_about.what: Indian dance — classical and folk — one move per object in "moves". The app reads this file directly: save it, reload the page. Every field name is checked, so a typo is reported with the file and move it is in.
_about.add: Copy a move that looks like the new one, paste it into "moves", give it a new id and change every field. Or: node scripts/catalog.js new <file> <id>  — writes a template with placeholder text to replace.
_about.remove: Delete the move's object (and the comma before or after it). Routines built in the app that used it will show it as missing.
_about.check: node scripts/catalog.js check  — or reload the app: a bad file shows the error on screen instead of the exercise list.
_about.names: Anything written as a word instead of an object — "metric": "knee", "template": "lean", "preset": "standing", "conditions": "balance" — is looked up in shared.json. Add reusable pieces there, not here.
_about.notes: Any field starting with "_" is a note for people and is ignored: "_note": "physio wants this re-checked".

fields.id: Unique name, used in links and saved sessions — never change it once the move has been used. Lower-case letters, digits, underscores. Good: "seated_knee_ext". Bad: "Seated Knee Ext", "knee-ext", "1_knee".
fields.name: What the user sees in the list. Good: "Seated knee extension". Bad: a clinical term nobody outside physio uses ("Open-chain terminal extension").
fields.clinicalName: Optional. The term a physio would use, shown in the details panel under the name.
fields.type: "reps" (counted) or "hold" (seconds in position). A stretch held for 30 s is a hold; ten slow raises are reps.
fields.view: "side" or "front" — where the phone stands. Side-on for anything that bends forward/back (knees, hips, spine); front-on for anything that goes out to the side (leg raise to the side, arm raise to the side, knees caving in).
fields.tracking: What the camera can honestly do: "form" (counts AND judges — needs at least one fault with a measurement and a threshold), "reps" (counts only; faults are listed for the person to watch), "none" (nothing to measure — the guide is shown and the set is logged by hand). Bad: "form" on a move whose faults are all words; the file will not load.
fields.vetted: Optional, true/false. true = a physio has recorded and checked this move in the Studio; vetted moves list first.
fields.equipment: List of words: ["none"], ["chair"], ["band", "door anchor"]. Optional extras say so: "ankle weight (optional)".
fields.muscles: { "primary": [...], "secondary": [...] } — plain names ("quadriceps", "gluteus medius"). primary must have at least one.
fields.sided: Only for one-sided moves: { "limb": "leg" | "arm" | "side", "by": "camera" | "pick", "auto": true }. "camera" = the limb nearest the phone is the working one (side-on moves); "pick" = the person chooses (front-on moves); "auto": true = when no side was chosen, watch both and follow the one that moves. Leave the field out for two-sided moves.
fields.upperBody: true when the legs need not be in frame (seated desk moves, shoulder work). Default false.
fields.summary: One line for the list. Good: "Sitting, straighten one knee until the leg is level, hold, and lower." Bad: a paragraph.
fields.setup: Where the phone goes and how to start, in the user's words. Good: "Sit tall on a chair, side-on to the phone, working leg nearest…" Bad: "Standard set-up."
fields.brief: What the coach SAYS out loud as the set begins: the position and the movement in one or two short sentences, no camera talk (the person has already placed the phone). Keep it under about 35 words — it is spoken while they get into position. Good: "Lie on your back, working leg straight. Slide the heel toward your bottom as far as it will go, then slide it back out." Bad: "Stand 2.5 m from the camera at hip height" (set-up, not movement) or a paragraph. Leave it out and the coach says only the name and the target.
fields.why: Why this camera angle can measure this move. Shown to the user; keeps the author honest. Good: "Side-on the knee angle runs from 90° to straight." Bad: left empty.
fields.calibrationPose: Optional. The still position held for the first two seconds of every set, which the coach measures against. Good: "Sitting tall, knee bent to 90°, foot hanging."
fields.camera: { "height": "floor" | "knee" | "hip" | "chest" | "eye", "distance": "2 m", "posture": "standing" | "sitting" | "lying" | "prone" | "sidelying" | "kneeling", "tolerance": 25 }. Leave it out to use the file's default at the top. posture also decides how the stick figure is pinned in place, and how a crooked phone is levelled at calibration (a standing or sitting trunk is upright, a lying one is along the floor; kneeling makes no assumption). tolerance: degrees the person may turn away from the ideal view mid-set before the coach says to turn back; leave it out for the settings.json default. Good: 20–30. Bad: 5 (nobody stands that still) or 60 (the joint is hidden by then).
fields.targets: Optional list of rep counts / hold seconds the bubble cycles through, e.g. [6, 8, 10, 12]. Leave it out for the standard choices in settings.json.
fields.defaultTarget: The one of targets selected to begin with. Must be in the list. Leave it out with targets.
fields.progress: How far through a rep the person is. { "metric": <measurement>, "start": "calibrated" | number, "target": number | "opt:rom" }. "calibrated" = whatever the measurement reads in the start position; "startMin"/"startMax" clamp it (a knee that calibrates at 150° is treated as 160°). target = the reading at a full rep, or with "targetIsDelta": true a change from the start — "delta": -1 when the reading goes DOWN during the rep (a knee angle closing). Only for type "reps" with tracking "form" or "reps". Good: knee angle from calibrated to 172. Bad: start and target the same number.
fields.show: What the coach asks the person to demonstrate once, before the set, so the target is measured on their body instead of assumed: { "ask": "arms straight out to the sides, level with your shoulders, nothing in your hands" }. They hold that pose still for a moment, with the band or weight out of the way, and what it reads becomes progress.target for the set. Only for a counted move, and only worth it when the number in progress.target depends on the body or the angle — a raise to shoulder height, a hands-apart distance — or when the equipment hides the joints. progress.target is still required: it is the fallback, and the sanity check (a demonstration under 40% or over 250% of it is refused). Good: one short sentence naming the end position. Bad: "do the exercise".
fields.hold: For type "hold" with tracking on: { "conditions": [ { "metric": <measurement>, "rel": "abs" | "change", "min": n, "max": n } ] } — the hold counts while every condition is met. "change" = relative to the calibrated start. A condition may carry "when": [{ "option": "variant", "is": "bent" }] so it only applies for that option. A named set ("balance") comes from shared.json.
fields.display: Optional. What the live readout shows: { "label": "bend", "unit": "°", "from": "start" } shows the progress measurement as a change from the start ("abs" = the raw reading); for a hold, { "condition": 0, "label": "knee", "aim": "90°" } shows that hold condition. Without it the app shows the raw progress reading.
fields.enterCue: Optional, holds only: what the coach says when the person has been out of position for a few seconds. Good: "Slide down the wall until your knees are at ninety".
fields.faults: What goes wrong, in the order they matter. Each: { "id", "label", "cue" (spoken, ≤ 8 words, what TO do), "tip" (written, why it matters), "severity" 1–3 }. Add "metric", "op" ("<" or ">"), "threshold" and the camera watches for it; leave those out and it is listed for the person to watch. "minP" (0–1) = ignore until this far into the rep; "persist" ms before it is spoken, "cooldown" ms before the same cue may repeat (rules included, so one that is true every rep is not said every rep); "rel": "change" compares to the calibrated start. "when": a list of gates that must all hold for the fault to count — { "option": "variant", "is": "bent" }, { "metric": <measurement>, "op": "<", "threshold": 168 }, "inPosition" or "notInPosition". "phase": "moving" / "rest" (reps) or "any" (a hold fault that must fire while the person is OUT of position; otherwise hold faults only watch the held position). "scale": { "metric": "progress", "times": 0.35 } makes the threshold grow with another reading. Rules instead of a measurement: "rule": "shallow" (rep did not reach the target), "fast" with "minMs", "return" with "threshold" (rep ended above this progress — did not come all the way back). Or "template": "lean" with a "threshold" to reuse one from shared.json. Good cue: "Sit tall". Bad cue: "You are leaning back again" (tells them what is wrong, not what to do).
fields.guide: { "surface": what to stand/lie on, "stop": when to stop, "cannotSee": what the person must check themselves, "regions": [ { "name": "Trunk", "points": [ { "t": "one form point", "tracked": true|false } ] } ] }. tracked: true only when a fault with a measurement actually checks that point — it is shown to the user as "camera watches".
fields.pose: The two-frame stick figure. { "A": start keyframe, "B": end keyframe, "work": { "thigh": 1, "glute": 0.5 } muscles to light up 0–1, "props": [ { "kind": "box" | "bar" | "disc" | "band", "at": "hip" } ], "wall": "behind" | "ahead", "anchor": joint(s) that stay put }. Side-view keyframe angles in degrees: torso (from vertical, + = leaning forward), thigh & shin (from hanging straight down, + = forward), foot (+ = toes up), uarm & farm (arms, + = forward), plus the far limb: thighF, shinF, footF, uarmF, farmF; face: "right" | "left". Front-view: legL, legR, shinL, shinR, armL, armR, foreL, foreR (+ = out to the side), lean, headTilt, squat 0–1. "preset": "standing" | "seated" | "supine" | "prone" | "quadruped" fills the usual values first. Check it on /figures.html.
fields.tempo: Free text. Good: "Up 2 s, hold 2 s, down 3 s."
fields.contraindications: When not to do it. Shown as "Do not do this if".
fields.sources: Optional list of { "name", "url" } added to the file's own sources.
fields.band: Optional. "none", "yellow", "red"… = offers the band-colour bubble with that default; true = offers it defaulting to none.
fields.minMs: Optional, reps only: the quickest a rep may take before "Too fast" fires (when the move lists no live fault of its own). Default in settings.json.
fields.options: Advanced: extra bubbles, e.g. a range target { "key": "rom", "label": "Range target", "values": [45, 60, 75, 90], "unit": "°", "default": 90 } referenced from progress.target as "opt:rom".
fields.figure: Advanced: point keyframes captured by the Studio instead of pose angles. Prefer pose.
fields.focus: Advanced: the landmark the live view highlights, e.g. "KNEE". Default: the last point of the progress measurement.
fields.group: Optional. The heading the move is listed under; default = the file's group at the top.
fields.region: Optional. The body region for filtering; default = the file's region.
fields.icon: Optional short label used where an icon is expected. Default "move".
fields.order: Optional. Position in the list; default = the file's order + position in this file.

sources.name: Upaj Academy — common mistakes beginners make in Kathak
Kalashri Academy — Kathak chakkars and technique
Foot postural deviations in female Kathak dancers

moves.name: Aramandi (half-sit)
moves.summary: The half-sitting stance every Bharatanatyam step is built on: heels together, knees open, spine tall.
moves.setup: Stand facing the phone about 2.5 m away, camera at hip height, whole body in frame. Heels together, toes turned out from the hips. Bend the knees straight out over the toes until the thighs drop about halfway, spine long, shoulders down. Hold.
moves.brief: Heels together, toes turned out from the hips. Bend the knees straight out over the toes until the thighs drop about halfway, spine long, shoulders down.
moves.why: Facing the camera shows both knees at once, so the depth of the sit and the turnout — the two things that make or break an aramandi — are both measured directly. The turnout of the feet is not: check that yourself.
moves.calibrationPose: Standing tall, heels together, before you sit into the stance.
moves.enterCue: Sit down into the stance — knees out over your toes
moves.tempo: Sit over 2 s, hold, rise over 2 s.
moves.dosage: 3 holds of 20–60 s, daily. Class warm-up: 5 minutes.
moves.progression: Longer holds; then muzhumandi (full sit) once the half-sit is easy.
moves.regression: Less depth; heels slightly apart; a hand on a wall.
moves.contraindications: Knee pain at the front, or a knee that will not turn out without the arch of the foot rolling in.

faults.label: Not sitting deep enough
faults.tip: The classic aramandi drops the thighs about halfway to horizontal. Higher than that and it is a standing pose.

faults.label: Knees falling forward
faults.cue: Open the knees over your toes
faults.tip: The turnout comes from the hip, not the knee or the foot. If the knees point forward the stance loses its shape and the arches roll in.

faults.label: Leaning forward to sit lower
faults.tip: Depth bought by tipping the chest forward is not depth. Keep the spine vertical and let the knees do the work.

faults.label: Tailbone sticking out
faults.tip: A duck tail arches the lower back and pushes the hips behind the heels. Draw the tailbone down so the pelvis sits under the ribs.

faults.label: Arches rolling inward
faults.tip: If the inner ankle collapses, the turnout is coming from the feet rather than the hips. Reduce the turnout until the arches hold.

faults.label: Shoulders creeping up
faults.tip: The effort belongs in the thighs. A raised shoulder line means you are bracing with the neck.

faults.label: Bobbing up and down
faults.tip: The hold is the training. Drifting up when it burns is the moment the quadriceps would otherwise be working.

guide.surface: Bare floor with grip, barefoot. Not carpet — the turnout needs the foot to sit flat.
guide.stop: Pain at the front or inside of the knee, or an arch that will not stop rolling in.
guide.cannotSee: How far the feet are actually turned out, and whether the turnout is coming from the hip or from the knee.

points.t: Heels touching, toes turned out as far as the hips allow — not as far as you can twist the feet.
Weight even across both feet; the inner arch stays lifted.
Bent straight out over the middle toe, making a diamond shape with the legs.
Thighs drop about halfway toward horizontal.
Spine long and vertical, ribs stacked over the pelvis, tailbone tucked.
Shoulders down and level, chest open.

moves.name: Tatta adavu (floor strikes)
moves.summary: The first adavu: hold aramandi and strike the floor with the flat of the foot, alternating, in time.
moves.setup: Face the phone about 2.5 m away, camera at hip height. Sit into aramandi and hold it. Lift one foot a few centimetres and strike the floor flat, sole slapping down as one piece, then the other. Count in fours.
moves.brief: Sit into aramandi and hold it. Lift one foot a few centimetres and strike the floor flat, the sole slapping down as one piece, then the other.
moves.why: The foot lifting and striking is a clear up-and-down the camera can count from the front. Whether the strike actually sounded, and whether the sole landed flat, it cannot hear or see.
moves.calibrationPose: Held in aramandi, both feet flat, before the first strike.
moves.tempo: Start slow — one strike per second. Speed comes later.
moves.progression: Double and quadruple speed; then the same in muzhumandi.
moves.regression: Stand tall instead of in aramandi; strike more slowly.
moves.contraindications: Heel or knee pain that builds; a hard floor without a mat if the joints are sensitive.

faults.label: Standing up out of the stance
faults.tip: The stance is held the whole time. Rising with each strike is the commonest way beginners save their thighs.

faults.label: Striking with the toes or heel first
faults.tip: The sound comes from the whole foot landing at once. Toe-first is a different adavu and a sore foot.

faults.label: Lifting the foot too high
faults.tip: A high lift breaks the rhythm and the stance. The foot barely leaves the floor.

faults.label: Chasing the speed
faults.tip: Uneven strikes at speed are worth less than even ones slowly. Match a beat you can hold.

faults.label: Arms drifting
faults.tip: The hands stay where the teacher placed them; drifting arms are a sign the legs are struggling.

guide.surface: Wooden or hard floor, barefoot. A thin mat if the joints are sensitive; never a thick carpet.
guide.stop: Pain in the heel, shin or knee that builds through the set.
guide.cannotSee: Whether the strike made a clean sound, and whether the sole landed flat.

points.t: Aramandi held throughout — the body does not rise between strikes.
Spine vertical, tailbone tucked, shoulders down.
The foot lifts only a few centimetres and lands as one flat piece.
The standing foot stays completely still.
Hands at the waist in kati hastam, elbows lifted and still.

moves.name: Natta adavu (heel strike, leg out)
moves.summary: From aramandi, stretch one leg out to the side and strike the heel, then bring it back with a flat strike.
moves.setup: Face the phone about 3 m away, camera at hip height, whole body and both arms in frame. From aramandi, extend one leg to the side with the knee straight and tap the heel, then draw it back and strike flat. Alternate.
moves.brief: From aramandi, extend one leg to the side with the knee straight and tap the heel, then draw it back and strike flat. Alternate.
moves.why: From the front the leg swings out across the camera plane, so the reach of each stretch is measured directly and counted.
moves.calibrationPose: Held in aramandi, both feet under you.
moves.tempo: Out 1 s, back 1 s, at a beat you can hold.
moves.progression: Faster tempo; deeper aramandi; add the arm positions.
moves.contraindications: Groin or inner-thigh pain; knee pain on the standing leg.

faults.label: Standing up as the leg goes out
faults.tip: The standing knee stays bent at the same depth the whole time. Rising is how the stretch gets longer without the work.

faults.label: Bending the stretched knee
faults.tip: The extended leg is straight with the heel leading; a bent knee makes the shape collapse.

faults.label: Leaning away from the leg
faults.tip: Tipping the trunk the other way makes the stretch look longer without the hip doing more.

faults.label: Leading with the toes
faults.tip: Natta adavu strikes the heel. Pointing the toe turns it into a different step.

faults.label: Hips turning with the leg
faults.tip: The pelvis stays square to the front; the leg goes out from the hip joint.

guide.stop: Groin pain, or a standing knee that aches after the set.
guide.cannotSee: Whether the heel strike sounded, and whether the toes stayed lifted.

points.t: Stays in aramandi at one height — the depth does not change.
Knee straight, heel leading, toes pulled up.
Out to the side in line with the body, not forward.
Upright and centred; hips square to the front.

moves.name: Chauka (Odissi square stance)
moves.summary: The square: feet wide and fully turned out, knees open, weight even — the masculine stance of Odissi.
moves.setup: Face the phone about 2.5 m away, camera at hip height. Feet a little wider than the hips and turned out, knees bent straight out over the toes, arms out to the sides at shoulder height with the elbows bent. The body makes a square. Hold.
moves.brief: Feet a little wider than the hips and turned out, knees bent straight out over the toes, arms out to the sides at shoulder height with the elbows bent. The body makes a square.
moves.why: From the front the two knee angles and the width between the knees are both direct reads, which is exactly what a chauka is judged on.
moves.calibrationPose: Standing tall, feet apart, before you sit into the square.
moves.enterCue: Sit into the square — knees wide over your toes
moves.tempo: Sit over 2 s, hold, rise over 2 s.
moves.progression: Longer holds; add the arm positions and head movements.
moves.contraindications: Knee or groin pain; hips that cannot turn out without the back arching.

faults.label: Not sitting deep enough
faults.tip: The chauka is a deep, even sit. A shallow version loses the square shape entirely.

faults.label: Knees closing in
faults.tip: The knees travel out over the toes to hold the square. Closing them puts the load on the inside of the knee.

faults.label: Weight sliding to one side
faults.tip: The square is symmetrical. A hip that drifts sideways means one leg is resting.

faults.label: Lower back arching
faults.tip: Arching to force more turnout moves the strain to the lower back. Reduce the turnout instead.

faults.label: Arms dropping
faults.tip: The arms hold their line at shoulder height for the whole hold — that is part of the stance.

guide.stop: Knee or groin pain; a lower back that will not stop arching.
guide.cannotSee: How far the feet are turned out, and whether the weight is truly even.

points.t: Feet wider than the hips, turned out from the hip joints.
Knees bent out over the toes, thighs opening to the sides.
Spine vertical, tailbone tucked, weight even on both feet.
Out to the sides at shoulder height, elbows bent, palms forward.

moves.name: Tatkar (Kathak footwork)
moves.summary: The flat-footed rhythmic footwork of Kathak: ta thei thei tat, at a tempo you can keep perfectly even.
moves.setup: Stand tall facing the phone, feet together, arms relaxed at the sides or in the classical position. Strike the floor with the flat of each foot in turn to the bol, keeping the body still above the waist. Practise at one tempo for the whole set.
moves.why: At speed the feet blur and the sound is the thing being judged — a phone can do neither. Set the timer, put the phone down, and log the practice.
moves.tempo: One tempo per set: vilambit (slow) before drut (fast).
moves.progression: Double then quadruple the tempo; add ghungroo; then longer compositions.
moves.regression: Slower tempo; shorter sets; softer floor.
moves.contraindications: Heel, shin or knee pain that builds — Kathak dancers are prone to foot and arch problems, so build the volume slowly.

faults.label: Going faster than you can keep even
faults.tip: Uneven fast tatkar teaches the wrong rhythm. Master the slow tempo before doubling it.

faults.label: Body bouncing with the feet
faults.tip: Everything above the hips stays quiet. A bobbing head or shoulders means the whole body is stamping.

faults.label: Bending the knees too much
faults.cue: Legs long, ankles do the work
faults.tip: Tatkar comes from the ankle and the flat of the foot, not from a squat.

faults.label: Landing on the ball or heel
faults.tip: The flat foot is what makes the sound. Ball-first is a different tradition and hard on the forefoot.

faults.label: Too much, too soon
faults.tip: Foot and arch problems in Kathak come from volume added faster than the feet adapt. Warm up, and add minutes weekly.

faults.label: Holding the breath
faults.tip: Long footwork sets are endurance work. Breathe with the cycle rather than holding it.

guide.surface: Wooden floor, barefoot. Never concrete for long sets.
guide.stop: Pain in the heel, arch, shin or knee that lasts after practice.
guide.cannotSee: Everything that matters here — the sound, the evenness, the bol. The phone times the practice.

points.t: The whole sole strikes flat; the lift is small.
Weight stays over the middle of the foot; arches stay lifted.
Tall and still above the waist — no bouncing.
Knees soft but not bent into a squat.
One tempo per set. Even beats matter more than fast ones.

moves.name: Chakkar (Kathak spins)
moves.summary: Continuous turns on the spot, spotting with the eyes, arms held in position.
moves.setup: Clear a space bigger than your arm span. Stand tall, arms out. Turn on the spot on the ball of one foot, pushing with the other, spotting a fixed point each turn. Build from four turns to sixteen.
moves.why: A spinning body faces away from the camera for most of every turn, so nothing can be measured. Time the practice and log it.
moves.tempo: Even turns; one spot per turn.
moves.dosage: 2–3 sets of 30–60 s, after a footwork warm-up.
moves.progression: More turns per set; faster; then chakkars within a composition.
moves.regression: Quarter turns; half turns; fewer in a row with a pause.
moves.contraindications: Dizziness that does not settle between sets, any inner-ear problem, or a recent ankle sprain.

faults.label: Not spotting
faults.tip: The head whips round last and returns to the same point. Without spotting the dizziness is unavoidable.

faults.label: Travelling across the floor
faults.tip: Drifting means the push is going sideways. Keep the supporting foot under the middle of the body.

faults.label: Arms flailing
faults.tip: The arms stay where the composition puts them; loose arms spin the shoulders out of line.

faults.label: Pushing through dizziness
faults.tip: Stop, stand still, look at one point. Continuing while dizzy is how dancers fall.

faults.label: Dropping the heel mid-turn
faults.cue: Stay tall on the ball of the foot
faults.tip: A heel that drops catches the floor and stops the turn dead — and twists the ankle.

guide.surface: Smooth floor with room to fall safely. Nothing within arm span.
guide.stop: Dizziness that lasts, nausea, or a stumble.
guide.cannotSee: Everything — the body turns away from the phone. This is a timer and a log.

points.t: Spot a fixed point: the head stays, then whips round last.
Turn on the ball of the supporting foot, heel lifted.
Stay on one spot; do not travel.
Held in position, close enough to control the spin.

moves.name: Garba — do taali (two claps)
moves.summary: The two-clap Garba basic: step, step, clap — the circle step everyone starts with.
moves.setup: Face the phone about 2.5 m away, camera at hip height, whole body and both arms in frame. Step to the side, bring the other foot behind, dip slightly and clap at chest height. Keep the rhythm even and stay light on the feet.
moves.brief: Step to the side, bring the other foot behind, dip slightly and clap. Keep the rhythm even and stay light on the feet.
moves.why: The hands coming together is the clearest thing in the frame from the front, so the claps are counted. The footwork pattern and the travel around the circle are yours to watch.
moves.calibrationPose: Standing with the hands apart at chest height, before the first clap.
moves.tempo: Start at a walking pace; speed up over the set as Garba does.
moves.progression: Faster tempo; deeper dip; add the tran taali (three-clap) pattern.
moves.contraindications: Knee pain on the dip; ankle or foot pain from repeated bouncing on a hard floor.

faults.label: Staying upright and stiff
faults.cue: Bend the knees — dip with the clap
faults.tip: Garba is a soft, bouncing step. Locked knees turn it into marching and jar the joints.

faults.label: Hands barely meeting
faults.tip: Open the arms out and bring them together at chest height. Small hand flicks lose the rhythm.

faults.label: Stamping flat-footed
faults.tip: Landing flat on a hard floor for several minutes is what makes the calves and shins sore afterwards.

faults.label: Rounding the shoulders
faults.tip: Long sets tire the upper back and the shoulders creep forward. Keep the chest lifted.

faults.label: Rhythm drifting
faults.tip: The step is on the beat and the clap on the count. Drifting turns the circle into a shuffle.

guide.surface: Any floor with a little give. Barefoot or soft shoes; a hard floor for long sets is what makes feet ache.
guide.stop: Knee pain on the dip, or shin pain that builds.
guide.cannotSee: The footwork pattern, the direction of travel and the turn of the wrists.

points.t: Step to the side, other foot behind, soft landings.
Stay light — the heel touches, it does not stamp.
Soft, dipping with each clap.
Open wide, then clap at chest height on the count.
Shoulders down, chest open.

moves.name: Garba — tran taali (three claps)
moves.summary: The three-clap Garba: a deeper dip and a clap low, so the legs work far harder than in do taali.
moves.setup: Face the phone about 2.5 m away, camera at hip height. Step, step, then bend the knees and clap low near the floor before rising to clap high. Keep the back long as you fold.
moves.brief: Step, step, then bend the knees and clap low near the floor before rising to clap high. Keep the back long as you fold.
moves.why: The claps are counted from the hands meeting. The low dip is where the legs work, and that is yours to feel.
moves.calibrationPose: Standing with the hands apart at chest height.
moves.tempo: Even and unhurried; the dip takes a beat of its own.
moves.progression: Deeper dip; faster tempo; longer continuous sets.
moves.regression: Shallower dip; keep both claps at chest height.
moves.contraindications: Knee pain in the deep dip; lower-back pain when folding.

faults.label: Rounding the back to reach low
faults.cue: Bend the knees, keep the back long
faults.tip: The low clap comes from bending the knees, not from folding the spine.

faults.label: Skipping the dip
faults.cue: Bend the knees on the low clap
faults.tip: Without the dip this is just do taali. The dip is where the legs are trained.

faults.label: Heels lifting in the dip
faults.tip: Rising heels mean the dip is going forward instead of down. Sit the hips back a little.

faults.label: Rushing the low clap
faults.cue: Give the dip a full beat
faults.tip: Snatching the low clap is how knees and backs get sore over a long night of Garba.

faults.label: Holding the breath
faults.tip: These are long, continuous sets. Breathing with the rhythm is what makes them last.

guide.surface: Floor with a little give; barefoot or soft shoes.
guide.stop: Knee pain in the dip, or lower-back pain.
guide.cannotSee: The depth of the dip and whether the back stayed long.

points.t: Knees bend for the low clap; heels stay down.
Long and flat as you dip — bend the knees, not the spine.
Clap low near the knees, then high — three in the cycle.

moves.name: Bhangra — dhamaal
moves.summary: The big open Bhangra step: arms up, shoulders bouncing, one knee driving up on each beat.
moves.setup: Face the phone about 3 m away, camera at hip height, whole body and both raised arms in frame. Arms up with the index fingers pointing to the sky. Drive one knee up to hip height on the beat, land soft, then the other. Shoulders bounce with it.
moves.brief: Arms up with the index fingers pointing to the sky. Drive one knee up to hip height on the beat, land soft, then the other.
moves.why: From the front the knee rises across the camera plane, so the height of each lift is measured and counted directly.
moves.calibrationPose: Standing tall with both arms up, before the first knee lift.
moves.tempo: One lift per beat; energetic but landed softly.
moves.progression: Faster tempo; add a hop on the standing leg; longer sets.
moves.regression: Lower knee lift; march instead of hop; no arms overhead.
moves.contraindications: Knee, ankle or back pain on landing; anyone told to avoid impact; shoulder pain holding the arms overhead.

faults.label: Knee not coming up
faults.cue: Drive the knee to hip height
faults.tip: Dhamaal is a big step. A small knee lift makes it a march and loses the character.

faults.label: Arching the back under the arms
faults.tip: Holding the arms overhead for minutes tends to arch the lower back. Brace the middle.

faults.label: Landing heavily
faults.tip: Ball, then heel, with the knee bending to absorb it. Flat heavy landings are what hurt the next day.

faults.label: Leaning back
faults.tip: Leaning back to get the knee higher shifts the load onto the lower back.

faults.label: Shoulders locked
faults.tip: The shoulder bounce is half of Bhangra. Stiff shoulders make it look and feel like a workout, not a dance.

guide.surface: Floor with give — a sprung floor, a mat, or grass. Trainers if the floor is hard.
guide.stop: Any pain on landing; shoulder pain with the arms up.
guide.cannotSee: The arm and wrist shapes, and the shoulder bounce.

points.t: Knee drives up toward hip height on the beat.
Land through the ball of the foot with a soft knee.
Tall with the ribs down; do not arch back under the raised arms.
Up and open, index fingers to the sky, shoulders loose and bouncing.

moves.name: Bhangra — jhummar
moves.summary: The slow, graceful Bhangra: a gentle knee bend and sway with the arms moving in circles, danced to a slower beat.
moves.setup: Face the phone with room around you. Soften the knees, sway from side to side on the beat, and circle the arms in front of the body. It is a flowing step, not a jumping one.
moves.why: The whole character is in the flow of the arms and the turn of the wrists, which a phone cannot judge. Set the timer and dance.
moves.tempo: Slow and continuous, on the beat.
moves.dosage: 2–4 minutes, often as a warm-up or a cool-down from dhamaal.
moves.progression: Longer; add the full arm patterns and turns.
moves.regression: Smaller sway; hands on the hips.
moves.contraindications: Knee pain in the bend; dizziness with the turns.

faults.label: Bouncing instead of flowing
faults.cue: Soften it — flow, do not bounce
faults.tip: Jhummar is the graceful one. If you are jumping, you are dancing dhamaal.

faults.label: Knees locked straight
faults.cue: Keep a soft bend in the knees
faults.tip: The gentle knee bend is what makes the sway travel through the body.

faults.label: Arms too small
faults.tip: The arms draw wide circles. Small arms make it look tentative and skip the shoulder work.

faults.label: Rounding forward
faults.cue: Chest open, look up and out
faults.tip: The head and chest stay lifted; this is an open, generous shape.

guide.surface: Any floor with space to move.
guide.stop: Knee pain, or dizziness on the turns.
guide.cannotSee: The arm circles and wrist turns that are the whole point of the step.

points.t: Knees softly bent, weight shifting side to side on the beat.
Wide, slow circles in front of the body; shoulders loose.
Tall and open; the sway comes from the hips, not a collapsing spine.

moves.name: Griva bhedha (neck warm-up)
moves.summary: The classical neck movements — side to side and turning — done slowly as a warm-up before any dance practice.
moves.setup: Sit or stand tall facing the phone, about 1.5 m away, camera at chest height. Slide the head from side to side (sundari), then turn it left and right, keeping the shoulders completely still.
moves.brief: Sit or stand tall. Slide the head from side to side (sundari), then turn it left and right, keeping the shoulders completely still.
moves.why: Facing the camera, the head sliding across the shoulder line is counted. Whether the movement is a slide or a tilt is too subtle for a phone to separate.
moves.calibrationPose: Sitting or standing tall, head centred, shoulders level.
moves.tempo: Two seconds each way; never fast.
moves.progression: Larger range once it is comfortable; add the eye movements.
moves.regression: Smaller range; seated with the back supported.
moves.contraindications: Dizziness, pain shooting into the arm, or any neck injury not yet assessed.

faults.label: Shoulders moving with the head
faults.tip: The shoulders stay square and level. If they follow the head, the movement has left the neck.

faults.label: Tilting instead of sliding
faults.tip: Sundari is a sideways slide, ears staying level — not a tilt of the head toward the shoulder.

faults.label: Moving too quickly
faults.tip: This is a warm-up for a joint with a lot of small structures. Speed is how people strain it.

faults.label: Forcing the end of the range
faults.tip: Warm-ups move through the easy range. Pushing into the end is a stretch, and a different thing.

guide.surface: Sitting tall on a stool, or standing.
guide.stop: Dizziness, or any pain or tingling into the arm.
guide.cannotSee: Whether the head is sliding or tilting, and the eye movements that go with it.

points.t: Slides sideways with the ears staying level; then turns left and right.
Chin stays level throughout — no nodding.
Square, level and completely still.

moves.name: Dancer's calf and arch release
moves.summary: After footwork: stretch the calf against a wall, then roll the arch under a ball, one foot at a time.
moves.setup: Stand facing a wall, side-on to the phone. Step one foot back, heel down, and lean in until the calf stretches. Hold. Then stand on a ball under the arch and roll it slowly from heel to toe.
moves.why: The calf stretch itself is coached elsewhere; this is the two-part cool-down and the phone just times it while you also work the arch, which it cannot see.
moves.tempo: Ease in over 5 s, hold, breathe.
moves.dosage: 2 × 45 s each side, after every footwork session.
moves.progression: Longer holds; add the bent-knee version for the deeper calf.
moves.regression: Shorter holds; less lean; no ball.
moves.contraindications: Sharp calf or Achilles pain, or a painful heel first thing in the morning that has not been assessed.

faults.label: Back heel lifting
faults.tip: If the heel lifts the stretch has gone. Step the foot closer to the wall until it stays down.

faults.label: Rolling the ball too hard
faults.tip: The arch responds to slow, moderate pressure. Grinding on a hard ball can inflame it.

faults.label: Skipping the cool-down
faults.cue: Two minutes now saves a week
faults.tip: Foot and calf problems in dancers come from volume without recovery. This is the cheapest insurance there is.

faults.label: Bouncing the stretch
faults.tip: A steady hold lengthens the muscle; bouncing makes it tighten to protect itself.

guide.surface: A wall, and a tennis ball or a small roller for the arch.
guide.stop: Sharp pain in the calf or Achilles.
guide.cannotSee: The arch rolling — that part is yours to feel.

points.t: Back leg straight, heel flat, hips travelling toward the wall.
Hold, breathe, no bouncing.
Roll slowly heel to toe with moderate pressure, about 30 s each foot.
